photo.title: A thatched ploughman's shelter with walling made from mokodi (wild sage) stems.
The burial place of Tsele Mothowamorena's (born 1914) father, marked out by branches. He cleans the area and splashes water over it, calling his name and asking for rain.

The homestead of Setswantsho Zingoro in Gabamutsha, in the molapo region west of Shorobe. The lolwapa fencing and walling is relatively fresh, since his wife hired a car to go into the central swamps to cut letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis), paying the driver half the load she cut.

Remains of a temporary shelter in domed or beehive style. This type of shelter was known as mogwafatshe and was used by people during the ploughing season for some shade and rest. It was made with bent acacia stems and covered with palm leaves and millet stems.

Homestead of Shomana Samorwa and Shashe Sakoi (nickname Shoeshine) in Gweghiri, a molapo farming area west of Shorobe. Shomana and Shashe had lived together for 14 years, although were not married. Shashe was born around 1921/2 and had worked in the mines in South Africa.

Woman weaving a storage basket from palm fronds, some dyed brown using bark and root of motsinsila plant. This lady was married to Rra Kesego (meaning Kesego's father) - proper name Mosaroze Moramenwa. Kesego was the mother of Boitlhoko Garebakwena, Christopher Morton's fieldwork assistant. It was in this homestead that Christopher Morton and his wife Catherine stayed whilst carrying out fieldwork in the molapo farming area west of Shorobe.
Portrait of Tsele Mothowamorena (born 1914) outside his sleeping hut. Tsele farmed the molapo area around Gweghiri.
Interior of sleeping hut belonging to Tsele Mothowamorena.
View of fenced compounds, possibly Shorobe village.
Boitlhoko Garebakwena, Morton's research assistant.

View of ruined and partially built huts using drinks cans as main walling material, in the plot belonging to Tumelo Samoxhose (born 1968), a Yeyi man living in Wenela Ward (visible in background). Tumelo's father was from Malawi and mother from Seronga. He migrated to Matlapaneng Ward in Maun in 1982, coming to Wenela in 1992.

Drinks cans collected as a main walling material, in the plot belonging to Tumelo Samoxhose (born 1968), a Yeyi man living in Wenela Ward. Tumelo's father was from Malawi and mother from Seronga. He migrated to Matlapaneng Ward in Maun in 1982, coming to Wenela in 1992.

Inside the lolwapa (courtyard) of Zira Bwezi, a Yeyi woman from Sankuyo, showing the entrance to a circular plan hut with drinks-can walling plastered with mud, in the plot of Zira Bwezi, a Yeyi woman from Sankuyo.

Two grandsons of Mosaroze Moramenwa (also known as Rra Kesego) ploughing with donkeys in the molapo (seasonal flood plain) at Gweghiri, west of Shorobe. The grandson holding the plough is Boitlhoko Kgalalo, the one leading the donkeys is Lekgoana Kgalalo. In years past, these fields would have been watered with seasonal flood waters from the Okavango delta, but the gradual lessening of flood waters reaching the area had meant that farmers were relying on seasonal rains only.

Mosaroze Moramenwa (also known as Rra Kesego) ploughing with donkeys in the molapo (seasonal flood plain) at Gweghiri, west of Shorobe. The grandson with white shoes is Boitlhoko Kgalalo, the one leading the donkeys is Lekgoana. In years past, these fields would have been watered with seasonal flood waters from the Okavango delta, but the gradual lessening of flood waters reaching the area had meant that farmers were relying on seasonal rains only.
Two huts, one with a lolwapa courtyard in front, made using letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis).

Huts in the compound of Kesego Ntema and her sisters in Morutseng, using lethlaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) for walling and fencing. The thatched rectilinear hut to right is where their grandmother sleeps, with a thatched kitchen and windscreen close by.
Homestead with fenced compound made from mopane wood poles.
Portrait of two of Bailelwa Gabanakgosi's children.
Boitlhoko Garebakwena (left) and a relative collecting morogo wa thepe plant growing in the areas around Matlapaneng ward in the rainy season. The leaves are cooked liked spinach.
Boitlhoko Garebakwena, Christopher Morton's field assistant.

Mosaroze Moramenwa (also known as Rra Kesego) with his crop of maize in the molapo (seasonal flood plain) at Gweghiri, west of Shorobe. In years past, these fields would have been watered with seasonal flood waters from the Okavango delta, but the gradual lessening of flood waters reaching the area had meant that farmers were relying on seasonal rains only.

Mosaroze Moramenwa (also known as Rra Kesego) with his crop of maize in the molapo (seasonal flood plain) at Gweghiri, west of Shorobe. In years past, these fields would have been watered with seasonal flood waters from the Okavango delta, but the gradual lessening of flood waters reaching the area had meant that farmers were relying on seasonal rains only.

At the homestead of Mosaroze Moramenwa (just visible seated in background) at Gweghiri. Left to right: Catherine Mary Morton; unknown (a friend); Boitlhoko Garebakwena, his brother Lekgoana (the grandsons of Mosaroze).

View of houses in the plot of Njiro Sakutcha, in Sanyedi ward, Maun. The concrete brick, 3-room building belongs to her first son, who works in the local council. The round hut painted green is now rented out to a non-family member.

The house of one of the daughters of Koi Kadisa, a Yeyi woman living in Sanyedi ward. The daughter had grown older and wanted her own house on the plot. Since she was working at one of the safari lodges (Maun Lodge) she wanted to use the same letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) that they regularly use for buildings since she liked it. She adapted the style of the house from one of the safari lodge buildings she stayed in at Maun Lodge.

Portrait of Kefilwe Hadisa in her plot in Sanyedi ward, outside a hut used to accommodate visiting relatives. Kefilwe is the niece of Koi Kadisa, who gave her this piece of land to build on some years after she came to Maun to go to school, from where she was born in Boyei.

A large concrete block house under construction in the plot belonging to the Garebakwena family in Wenela ward. Morton's fieldwork assistant, Boitlhoko Garebakwena, lived here and contributed some of the money he earned towards the costs of the house. Multi-room houses of this size were quite unusual in most wards of Maun at the time.

View of houses in the family area of Oteng Solomon, a Yeyi woman living in Sanyedi ward and niece of Solomon Samatshwa by a different father. The hut to the left is used by his aunt's daughter, the one in the middle is hers, and the one to the right is her younger sister's (emang).

Moeti Motho, a Yeyi man living in Sanyedi ward, sitting outside his courtyard fence lolwapa made from letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis). He used to have a lot of cattle but after lung disease he used the compensation payments to build. The other side of him is the house and lolwapa of his wife's mother who has come to live with them, and the round mud brick hut to the right belongs to his son. The plot in general is especially well kept and maintained, with renewed letlhaka courtyard fencing that many found increasingly expensive to buy.
An elderly man in the household of Odirilwe Mbwe in Sanyedi ward.
An elderly man in the household of Odirilwe Mbwe in Sanyedi ward.

View of the exterior of the surrounding lolwapa courtyard fence made from letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis), at the home of Naroxoh Mayezi, a Yeyi woman living in Mabadutsa ward. A shade shelter is just visible to left.

Christopher Morton with Khana Zambo, a Yeyi woman living in Mabadutsa ward. Khana was born in 1905 and came to Maun many years ago from Tsau village, and was here by the time Kgosi Moremi III died (1946) she said.
A small store for thatching grass made from mopane poles (maphako) in the home of Ditshupelo Sanyame, a Yeyi man living in Sankuyo village.

A cat sleeping on blankets in the shade of a lolwapa fence, inside the courtyard surrounding the hut where children or visitors sleep. Part of the home of Ditshupelo Sanyame, a Yeyi man living in Sankuyo village.

A partially ruined house made from mud brick and drinks cans, in the home of Ditshupelo Sanyame, a Yeyi man living in Sankuyo village. This combination of walling in rectilinear form is inherently weak and susceptible to collapse following heavy rains.

Catherine Morton and another woman soaking moretlhwa (brandy bush, Grewia flava) berries to make an alcoholic beverage for the wedding of Mosaroze Moramenwa, which was being celebrated at the home of his daughter Kesego Kgalalo in Maun. Kesego was the mother of Boitlhoko, Morton's fieldwork assistant.

Family members in celebratory mood for the wedding of Mosaroze Moramenwa, which was being celebrated at the home of his daughter Kesego Kgalalo in Maun. Kesego was the mother of Boitlhoko (left), Morton's fieldwork assistant. With him are two of his sisters (one to right is Botšale) and his father Rra Kgalago.

Women in traditional tšale (shawl) and tuka (headscarf) at the wedding celebrations of Mosaroze Moramenwa in the newly made lolwapa of his daughter Kesego Kgalalo in Wenela ward, Maun. Kesego was the mother of Boitlhoko, Morton's fieldwork assistant. Catherine Morton joined the women and Christopher Morton sat with the men.

Mosaroze Moramenwa with his new wife, at the home of his daughter Kesego Kgalalo in Wenela ward, Maun. Kesego was the mother of Boitlhoko, Morton's fieldwork assistant. The Mortons' marriage gift was the shoes that Mosaroze is wearing. The bride is wearing traditional tšale (shawl) and tuka (headscarf).

Mosaroze Moramenwa with his new wife, flanked by two other female relatives, at the home of his daughter Kesego Kgalalo in Wenela ward, Maun. Kesego was the mother of Boitlhoko, Morton's fieldwork assistant. The women are wearing traditional tšale (shawl) and tuka (headscarf).

Mosaroze Moramenwa with his new wife, flanked by two other female relatives, at the home of his daughter Kesego Kgalalo in Wenela ward, Maun. Kesego was the mother of Boitlhoko, Morton's fieldwork assistant. The women are wearing traditional tšale (shawl) and tuka (headscarf).
A woman weaving letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) into a new courtyard fence, part of preparations for the wedding of Mpho Bojosi to his girlfriend Kagiso.

A cooking shelter with a windbreak incorporating drinks cans and concrete plaster, in the plot of Keokeditswe Sarefo, a Yeyi woman living in Matumo ward. Sometimes people used wet concrete like this, in a similar manner to mud, without realising that the concrete would burn their skin. A number of people told me that they had burned their hands in this manner.

Kesego Kgalalo (in yellow shawl) with her children and grandchildren. Kesego was the mother of Morton's fieldwork assistant Boitlhoko. The girl in the pink dress is Bonana. The son standing behind Kesego is Lekgoana, and the son standing second from right is Dombas. Her daughter Botšale is holding her new baby Gaorethoa.
Botšale, the daughter of Kesego Kgalalo, with her baby Gaorethoa.
Friends and relations of Mpho Bojosi, on his wedding day.
Male friends at the wedding of Mpho Bojosi to Kagiso, in the Bojosi plot in Wenela ward.
Maikano Dipuo making a basket, now in the museum collection.
Hut in the Shorobe molapo area.

A store hut in the molapo area around Totoga near Shorobe village, unusually using stalks of maize crop for walling material. The owner was elderly, without money to buy letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) from the central Okavango swamp area.
Concrete house with letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) lolwapa fence in Saphane Ward, Maun.

The homestead of Tsele Mothowamorena (born 1914), a Yeyi man living in the Gweghiri molapo area near Shorobe village. The homestead includes huts for his cousin in foreground (daughter of his paternal uncle) and nephew in far distance.

The homestead of Tsele Mothowamorena (born 1914), a Yeyi man living in the Gweghiri molapo area near Shorobe village. The homestead includes huts for his cousin in foreground (daughter of his paternal uncle) and nephew in far distance.
A baobab tree in the background and in the foreground a burial site marked with upright sticks.
Portrait of Dash Maphomo outside his house in Gabamutsha, a molapo farming area west of Shorobe.
Homestead of Dash Maphomo in Gabamutsha, a molapo farming area west of Shorobe.

A sleeping hut with lethlaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) fencing either side of the entrance. The walling is made from drinks cans collected from a local bar (ntlo ya ditini). In the homestead of Mpepi Morapedi, a Yeyi woman from Shorobe now living in Wenela Ward.
A circular hut with walling made from drinks cans collected from a local bar (ntlo ya ditini). In the homestead of Mpepi Morapedi, a Yeyi woman from Shorobe now living in Wenela Ward.
